title: Bangla Sahib
hook: in Delhi, the gurdwara of the child Guru, with its healing pool

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akal Takht today, new stone on old ground, facing the Harmandir across the courtyard. Your line was facing each other. Before which decision did you stop and listen first? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

A plastic bottle, the kind you'd buy at any corner shop, sits on a kitchen shelf in a Delhi apartment. Nobody drinks from it casually. It was filled at the edge of a pool in the middle of the city, carried home on the metro, and it's kept for when someone in the house is unwell. A grandmother will pour a little into a steel cup and hand it over without a word. The pool is at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, a short walk from one of the city's big traffic circles. Year one told how the child Guru came to Delhi. Today, the place he left behind, and the water.
screen: `A BOTTLE ON A KITCHEN SHELF.` → `KEPT FOR WHEN SOMEONE IS UNWELL.` → `FILLED AT A POOL IN DELHI.`

segments.voice: First, the house. Bangla means bungalow. Tradition says Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru and still a child, stayed here in the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh when he was called to Delhi. While he was there, an epidemic swept the city, and the child went out among the sick of every faith, as year one told. He caught the disease himself and died in Delhi. The bungalow became a gurdwara. Second, the water. Tradition says the house's well gave the water the young Guru blessed and handed to the sick. Today a wide pool, a sarovar, lies beside the gurdwara, and people come to sit by it, to touch the water to their eyes, and to fill bottles to take home. Some Sikhs add a caution: the water isn't a charm; what it carries is the memory of a child who served. That's the healing pool. Third, a hymn that makes the story deeper. In the Granth, in Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan gives thanks, here in paraphrase: the Beloved has given protection from smallpox; the Supreme Lord has shown mercy. Tradition links that hymn to Guru Arjan's own young son, the boy who would become Guru Hargobind, when he fell ill. So, as tradition reads it, the Granth holds a father's relief over a sick child. At Bangla Sahib the story turns around. Here it's the child who goes to the sick. Fourth, why a child's gurdwara matters. Sikhs say the same light passed from Guru to Guru, whatever the body's age. At Bangla Sahib you can see what that light did in a small body: it didn't hide from a sick city. That's today's line: the child's gurdwara.
screen: `BANGLA: A RAJA'S BUNGALOW.` · `A POOL FOR THOSE WHO ARE UNWELL.` · `GURU ARJAN'S THANKS FOR A SICK CHILD.` · `THE LIGHT IN A SMALL BODY.` · then, large: `THE CHILD'S GURDWARA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the pool. Settle, and breathe. See the wide water, the white building and the gold dome above it, the steps going down to the edge. See people sitting there quietly, someone dipping a hand, someone filling a bottle for a person at home. Now bring to mind one person you know who is unwell. Picture sitting beside them for a moment. Just that. Stay there with them for a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Bangla Sahib. The gurdwara in Delhi at the bungalow where tradition says Guru Har Krishan stayed and served the sick, with its pool beside it. Today's word.
Your line: the child's gurdwara. Today, check on one person who is unwell, with a message or a call, and ask what would actually help. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Visitors to Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, eat in the langar, and sit by the sarovar; some take its water home for family members who are unwell.

notes: Days 73, 617 and 689 told the epidemic, the Ardas line and the succession; today's new angle is the pool as people use it now, and Guru Arjan's hymn on Ang 620.

Ang 620 (Sorath M5, 'seetlaa te rakhiaa bihaaree, paarbraham prabh kirpaa dhaaree') is traditionally linked to the child Hargobind's recovery from smallpox. Please confirm Ang and that the tradition links it to Hargobind.
'Sikhs speak of it carefully: the water itself is not a medicine' is a fair-sounding summary of Sikh teaching against charms, but not sourced; please confirm the wording.

The hook (bottles filled at the sarovar and kept at home for the sick) is a general description of practice; please confirm it is fair. 'A short walk from one of the city's big traffic circles' means as Connaught Place but is not named; cut if inaccurate.
'Bangla means bungalow' was also stated on day 689.

Editor pass: cut 'a generation before' (wrong span: Hargobind was Har Krishan's grandfather); the hymn now says only what it says (protection from smallpox) and the link to the child Hargobind is framed as tradition; 'Sikhs speak carefully: the water is not a medicine' (a claim for all Sikhs) softened to 'some Sikhs add a caution', and the matching myth item replaced; practice and carry no longer hand over a glass of water, which day 1331 uses.
